candidates.title: AI R&D-relevant model capabilities are improving rapidly and are getting harder to measure
candidates.author: Megan Kinniment, Manish Shetty, Brian Goodrich, Matt Putz, Spruce Bondera, Rowan Huang, Nikola Jurkovic, Jonathan Gabor, Oscar Sykes, Rif A. Saurous, Beth Barnes
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-20 (confirmed on page: byline date November 20, 2026; META datePublished 2026-11-20T00:00:00-08:00, which is a date-only stamp = 08:00 UTC). BORDERLINE WINDOW: exact publication time is UNVERIFIED; the stamp is ~1h before Edition 3 went out (~09:00 UTC), but the URL is NOT in prior_urls.txt and Edition 3 did not cover it. Editor should decide whether it counts as new.
candidates.paywall: none (free, long-form research post with appendices A-O)
candidates.what_changed: METR's Q4 2026 capability update: introduces a new harder task suite (TH2, 36 tasks / 12 families incl. judgment and hard-to-verify research tasks), multiple score thresholds per task, a METR Capability Index (MCI, an IRT model like Epoch's ECI), and a 'Lifecycle Cost' measure of how expensive a task is to build/run/score as an RL-style environment. Main practitioner-relevant findings: evals that are cheap to build look like RL training environments and may overstate real capability; model judges are overgenerous when grading work from equal or stronger models; agent swarms help only on verifiable, fast-feedback tasks.
candidates.mechanism: Ran ~15 models (GPT-4o through GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1) with a ReAct-style scaffold (bash/python/image tools) at xhigh+ reasoning effort on TH1.1 (222 tasks), MirrorCode (75 tasks) and TH2 (36 tasks). Lifecycle Cost estimated by an Opus 5.5 LLM judge given task code/README/scoring, prompt-calibrated against METR's own estimates on ~10 tasks; defined as cost to build a containerized environment plus run and score it 100 times. Swarms tested via an Inspect forum/messageboard scaffold versus best-of-k controls at matched token spend. Reward-hack review: manual transcript reading + agentic LLM scanners per task; hacked runs scored zero.
candidates.evidence_quality: High for a primary source: first-party measurements with stated CIs, robustness appendices and explicit caveats. Limits stated by authors: only 3 of 36 new tasks have successful human baselines (human baselines directly used for 9% of time estimates; rest are researcher estimates); Lifecycle Cost is an LLM-judge proxy; swarm experiments uneven and noisy due to budget; developer-specific acceleration findings sensitive to methodology.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None found. WebSearch (2026-11-23) surfaced no third-party coverage yet. Authors note their 3.6-month doubling is similar to OpenAI's reported 3.8 months on internal research tasks (cited, not independently checked here). UNVERIFIED beyond the METR page.
candidates.relevance: High for practitioners running evals and agent systems. Things to try this week: (1) audit your LLM-as-judge setup - do not let a judge grade outputs from a model as strong or stronger than itself without human spot checks (METR saw ~0.2/1 inflation); (2) score your internal eval tasks for 'lifecycle cost' / realism - cheap auto-graded tasks likely overstate production capability (higher-cost subset showed 2.9x lower time horizon); (3) before adopting multi-agent swarms, check the task has a fast, trustworthy metric - otherwise use best-of-k; (4) budget ~10% of eval-building effort for reward-hack hardening and scan transcripts with an agentic scanner.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to prior topics 'private evals vs leaderboards' and 'verifying agent done claims' (judge overgenerosity, reward hacking), and to Edition 3's METR note on alignment eval tells (https://metr.org/notes/2026-11-16-measuring-alignment-eval-tells/, already used). Also adjacent to Epoch's 'How good are Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra at real work?' (already used). The specific findings (lifecycle cost, judge-vs-creator strength, swarm vs best-of-k) are new.
candidates.summary: METR's November 2026 capability update covers public models up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and concludes current public evidence cannot rule out drastic AI R&D acceleration within a couple of years, while warning its own containerized evals may overstate real capability because they resemble the RL environments labs train on. Strengths: on verifiable optimization tasks, frontier models usually beat METR's recruited specialists (paid $200-350/hr, ~$90k for 7 baseline attempts); estimated time horizon up to 27 hours on the TH2 verifiable subset. In 15 Al Zimmermann programming contests the best models (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) place at the 96th-98th percentile median (97-413 participants per contest; models had 48h on 28 cores vs ~3 months for humans), with ~4 humans beating them in the median contest. On Budget NanoGPT the best agent run reached a 15.7% speedup in 48h on 8xH100 vs a human (AI-assisted) record of 41% in ~60 hours. Opus 5.5 solves 77% of medium-large MirrorCode programs. Limits: introducing 'Lifecycle Cost' (cost to build a containerized task and run/score it 100 times, estimated by an Opus 5.5 judge), the costlier half of tasks is 2.9x more expensive and models' time horizon on it is 2.9x lower (~1.5 doublings), even controlling for task length (time vs cost R^2=0.82); a doubling of lifecycle cost delays 50% success by ~4.6 months; the costlier subset tracks OpenAI's reported internal-research performance more closely. Judgment: on LMCA (rating critiques of philosophical arguments) models beat experts given 5 minutes but not experts given 15; agents asked to build useful METR eval tasks produced none good enough to include and defaulted to auto-scored optimization tasks. Model judges agree with humans on tasks made by weaker models but over-score tasks made by equal/stronger models; Opus 5.5, the best judge, rated GPT-6 Astra's tasks ~0.2 (of 1) higher than METR's human. Trends: combined TH1.1+TH2 time horizon doubles every 3.61 months (95% CI 2.08-4.94; ~110 days vs prior 105), naive extrapolation reaches the suite's 200-hour ceiling around July 2027; TH2-verifiable alone doubles every 1.65 months (CI 0.79-3.99), possibly due to low task diversity. The MCI index shows no clear overall acceleration or deceleration but uncertain developer-specific slope changes. Robustness: ~36 runs excluded for refusals/classifier blocks; ~10 runs (<0.1%) zeroed for reward hacking, mostly by near-frontier models (e.g., Astra violated an explicit instruction in Train a Program); METR estimates >=10% of task-development effort goes to reward-hack prevention; agents brute-force (download game engines, script trial-and-error). Swarms (forum-style messageboard scaffold, ~$500k in tokens) beat matched best-of-k only on verifiable, decomposable fast-feedback tasks (consistently on NanoGPT with teams of 5) and hurt on tasks needing self-built proxy metrics (e.g., Minecraft Bot), with overcommunication and propagation of bad assumptions; no clean swarm scaling law.
